title: Psychological, physiological, and phenomenological effects of colored light
research_question: How can we design with colored light in deliberate, controlled ways?
What is a person's response to being bathed in colored light, and how can we provide a positive phenomenological experience?
How can this research be applied effectively in an interior design project?
study_design: Mixed-methods research including a literature review, creative explorations with small-scale models, and a pilot user study in an immersive light room. The findings inform a conceptual design project.
setting: Laboratory (5'x9' room for pilot study), conceptual day spa design

participants.demographics: Recruited from design studios within the School of Design + Construction at Washington State University.

intervention_exposure: Participants spent five minutes alone in a 5'x9' room with no natural light, equipped with two 30' long RGB LED tape lights (at 2' and 6' heights) and white paper walls. They used a remote to control the color and intensity of the lights.
outcome_measures: Self-reported enjoyment of the experience (interview questions)
Perceived calming/stimulating effects of different colors (interview questions)
Qualitative feedback on the ability to control light color and intensity (interview questions)
Qualitative feedback on reactions to specific colors (interview questions)

key_findings.consequent: physiological effect (e.g., electroencephalogram, galvanic skin response, blood pressure, heart rate, respiration rate, eyeblink frequency)
key_findings.quote: color has a physiological effect on us, whether we perceive it visually or not. Kaiser asserts that “physiological human responses to color as evidenced by the electroencephalogram, galvanic skin response, blood pressure, heart rate, respiration rate, and eyeblink frequency...”
red light has been found to prevent scar tissue
monochrome light domes are used to treat phobias, depression and stress
blue light is used to treat jaundice in infants
Research indicates that color has an effect on our mood
Research has correlated emotional reactions to and psychological associations with color hue, saturation, and brightness.
The color red has been associated with excitement, anger, passion
orange has been perceived as distressing and upsetting
purple as dignified and stately
bright yellow as cheerful
blue has been associated with comfort
green as having a calming effect

key_findings.consequent: biological basis (e.g., red's long wavelengths leading to intense physiological reactions)
key_findings.quote: psychological responses to color are biologically based (i.e. red is associated with strong, highly stimulating emotions, possibly because the wavelengths of red light are longer, penetrate the skin more deeply, and produce more intense physiological reactions), but they are also based on learned associations of color meaning
color itself plays a strong role in our experience of place – in the essence of our existence.

key_findings.consequent: connection to memory, sense of place, self-identity, trigger for recollection of experience, gateway to a multisensory experience
key_findings.quote: Since color is tied to memory, and is connected to our sense of place, of self-identity, and is a trigger for recollection of experience, color itself is a gateway to a multisensory experience, and can be used in strategic ways in design.

key_findings.antecedent: user-controlled immersive colored light room experience
key_findings.quote: of the 22 participants, 100% claimed to enjoy the experience.

key_findings.antecedent: ability to change color and intensity of lights (user control)
key_findings.quote: The ability to change the color and intensity of the lights was cited by many as a positive aspect to study.
When asked which color felt calming and which color felt stimulating, their answers varied dramatically.
Some felt calm in a white room, since they are used to that color of light.
Certain colors, such as red, elicited strong reactions – some positive and some negative.
Blue also had varying responses.

key_findings.source: 3 Application to a conceptual design project
key_findings.quote: This study informed that people do enjoy being bathed in colored light but need to be in control of the color and intensity.

key_findings.antecedent: user control of color and intensity
key_findings.consequent: enjoyment of being bathed in colored light
key_findings.source: 3 Application to a conceptual design project
key_findings.quote: This study informed that people do enjoy being bathed in colored light but need to be in control of the color and intensity.

key_findings.consequent: categorization of design outputs (Painting with Light, Immersion in Light, Capturing Light)
key_findings.quote: Three categories of design outputs were identified, which were labeled Painting with Light, Immersion in Light, and Capturing Light.

key_findings.consequent: taxonomy of designing with colored light
key_findings.quote: The findings of this research phase include the categorization of design outputs as well as a taxonomy of designing with colored light (Fig. 3).

limitations: It is not possible to confirm that the designed spaces would have physiological effects on visitors; a more complete and controlled study is needed.
The degree of physiological response to proposed designs is uncertain.
The psychological effects of colored light are not clearly known, representing a gap in research.
The pilot study's five-minute exposure duration is insufficient to determine if longer exposure would lessen enjoyment.

findings.consequent: Physiological responses (blood pressure, eye-blink frequency) and psychological responses (mood, emotional reactions to hue, value, chroma)
findings.summary: Existing research indicates that exposure to colored light has layered effects on human physiological responses, such as changes in blood pressure and eye-blink frequency, and psychological responses, including mood and emotional reactions to specific color attributes.
findings._original_effect_size: Not quantified in paper, qualitative evidence from literature review
findings._quarantine_reason: Effect size is not numeric: 'Not quantified in paper, qualitative evidence from literature review'

findings.consequent: Role in experience of place, connection to memory and self-identity, gateway to multisensory experiences
findings.summary: Color plays a significant role in the human experience of place, being deeply tied to memory and self-identity, thereby serving as a gateway to engaging multisensory experiences in built environments.
findings._original_effect_size: Not quantified in paper, qualitative evidence from literature review

findings.consequent: Enjoyment and positive perception of control
findings.summary: A pilot study found that 100% of 22 participants universally enjoyed a user-controlled immersive colored light experience, particularly valuing the ability to change the light's color and intensity.
findings._quarantine_reason: Effect size is not numeric: '100% of 22 participants claimed enjoyment'

findings.consequent: Perceived calming/stimulating effects and emotional reactions
findings.summary: Participant responses regarding which colors felt calming or stimulating, and the emotional reactions elicited by specific colors like red, varied dramatically in an immersive light room setting, indicating subjective psychological effects.
findings._quarantine_reason: Effect size is not numeric: 'Varied dramatically among participants'

paper_metadata.title: Psychological, physiological, and phenomenological effects of colored light
paper_metadata.crossref_title: Psychological, physiological, and phenomenological effects of colored light
paper_metadata.crossref_abstract: This research explores colored light from historical, scientific, and technological vantage points. Effects of colored light on the human condition are examined on multiple levels, comparing theories in physiological, psychological, and phenomenological areas of study, addressed across a broad scope of literature. The focus of this research is to gain an understanding of the effects of colored light on the human condition, and how designing with it can provide an engaging phenomenological experience which marries centuries’ old design techniques with modern technological innovations. The stages of research include a literature review, followed by a series of creative explorations with light, texture and form through small-scale models. Data gathered is then analyzed, categorized, and used to create a taxonomy for designing with colored light. Research is then explored on a larger scale through a pilot study conducted in a 5’ x 9’ room designed to create an experience of being bathed in colored light with user-controlled variability. Each research method may then be used to inform the design of interior environments, affecting the participant’s physiological, psychological, and phenomenological experiences.
